description: We are second-year ECE engineering students from VCET, Erode, working on the "Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts" challenge. Our focus is edge AI and explainable AI: an offline, on-board health monitor that detects anomalies in astronaut vitals and explains why each alert fired. We are looking for teammates skilled in web development, data visualization, graphic design, data analysis, and communications to help build the dashboard and pitch.
summary: AstraHeart is an offline-first web app that helps astronauts assess their own health on long missions, when help from Earth is delayed. Crew members log heart rate, blood pressure, glucose, temperature, sleep, mood, symptoms, exercise, cabin CO2 and radiation dose through a clickable body map and a daily check-in. The app compares each reading with the astronaut's personal baseline, shows Green/Yellow/Red status, explains in plain language why a result changed, and links findings to NASA's five spaceflight hazards. It gives step-by-step actions, a what-if simulator, 30-day trend charts, and one of three escalation levels (self-manage, notify crew, contact flight surgeon), with a handoff report queued for the flight surgeon under a simulated Mars communication delay. On Moon and Mars missions, crews cannot wait minutes or hours for medical advice, so clear, explainable, offline guidance matters. AstraHeart is a prototype: it uses general clinical reference ranges and rule-based scoring, not NASA flight limits, and has not been validated on astronaut data.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

AstraHeart is a decision-support tool for astronauts who must monitor their own health far from Earth. NASA's Human Research Program identifies five spaceflight hazards (radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, and hostile/closed environments). AstraHeart turns daily health readings into clear guidance for those risks.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Interactive body map: the home screen shows a clickable body with 17 regions (heart, lungs, brain, eyes, bones, muscles, immune system and more). Each region shows its status, its linked spaceflight hazard, an "Earth connection", and what the crew member can do.

2. Daily check-in: heart rate, blood pressure, glucose, temperature, sleep, mood, exercise, cabin CO2, radiation dose and symptoms. Inputs are validated, and each astronaut has an editable personal baseline.

3. Analysis: every indicator gets a Green/Yellow/Red status with an icon and label. A readiness score, a prototype cardiac risk estimate and a drift-from-baseline value summarize the result. A "why this result" breakdown explains the main contributors in plain language.

4. Guidance: step-by-step actions, a what-if simulator (for example, how more sleep or exercise changes the estimate), and three escalation levels: self-manage, notify crew, contact flight surgeon.

5. Distance from Earth: a Mars/Moon/ISS environment selector and a communication-delay slider. Reports are queued locally (nothing is transmitted) in a one-page handoff summary for the flight surgeon.

6. Trends and demo tools: 30-day charts with a mission-day scrubber, a Mars Transit Day 140 scenario, a Judge mode with sample data, and a simulated wearable sync.

7. Evidence: each panel links to NASA Human Research Program pages on the matching hazard or risk.

BENEFITS

It works with no internet connection, explains every alert in plain language so crew do not need medical training, and gives a safe first step before ground contact is possible.

TOOLS

HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript in a single offline web page; SVG and canvas graphics; browser localStorage; hosted on GitHub Pages; built in VS Code with AI coding assistance (see the SI section).

LIMITATIONS (honest scope)

This is a concept prototype. Thresholds are general clinical reference ranges, not NASA flight limits. Scoring is rule-based and is not a trained model. The wearable sync and image upload are simulated. Data is stored only in the browser and is not secured to medical-data standards. It has not been validated on astronaut data.

FUTURE WORK

Flight-surgeon-defined limits, validation with NASA mission and open data, real sensor integration, medical-grade privacy and security, and testing with crew-like users.
